summary: This R documentation page describes the varTest function in the EnvStats package, which performs a one-sample chi-squared test on a population variance, assuming normality, and returns a confidence interval for the variance. It explains the arguments (alternative, conf.level, sigma.squared, data.name), notes that the chi-squared variance test is very sensitive to non-normality unlike the t-test for location, and gives an example testing whether the variance of 20 simulated normal observations equals 0.5. The example yields an estimated variance of 0.753708 and a p-value of 0.1436947, so the null is not rejected at the 5% or 10% level.
one_line: Documentation for EnvStats' varTest function, a chi-squared test of a single population variance with a confidence interval, assuming normal data.
key_facts: varTest is a function in the EnvStats package that performs a one-sample chi-squared test on variance.
The varTest function estimates the variance, tests the null hypothesis that the variance equals a user-specified value, and creates a confidence interval for the variance.
The default value of the sigma.squared argument in varTest is 1.
The alternative argument defaults to "two.sided" and may also be "greater" or "less".
The R function var.test performs the F-test for comparing two variances.
The documentation states that the chi-squared test on the population variance is extremely sensitive to departures from normality.
The documentation states that if the underlying population is skewed, the actual Type I error rate of the variance test will be larger than assumed.
Student's t-test is described as fairly robust to departures from normality for a one-sample test of location when the sample size is reasonably large.
The documentation lists two methods for a one-sample test on variability: the chi-squared method assuming normality, and a bootstrap confidence interval method using, for example, the boot package.
The example generates 20 observations from a normal distribution with mean=2 and sd=1 using set.seed(23).
In the example, the null hypothesis is that the true variance equals 0.5, tested against the alternative that it does not.
The example output gives an estimated variance of 0.753708 and a Chi-Squared test statistic of 28.64090 with df = 19.
The example output gives a P-value of 0.1436947 and a 95% confidence interval of LCL = 0.4359037 and UCL = 1.6078623.
The author of the page is Steven P. Millard.
